lesson.title: The Event Horizon: A Boundary Light Cannot Cross Outward
lesson.objective: Explain why light moves at its usual speed locally yet cannot escape from inside an event horizon.
lesson.approachReason: Testing the claim that gravity stops light reveals that the event horizon limits where a signal can go, not how fast it moves nearby.

blocks.heading: Light does not run out of speed
blocks.body:
The event horizon is the boundary beyond which signals cannot reach distant space. It is not a surface that stops light. An astronaut falling through it would still measure a nearby beam moving at the usual speed of light.

The question is not whether light can move. It is where the beam’s path can lead.
blocks.example: For a sufficiently large black hole, crossing the horizon need not feel like hitting anything.

hints: The astronaut measures the beam nearby on both sides of the boundary.
Ask what crossing changes: the local measurement or the places a signal can eventually reach?
blocks.retry: Imagine drawing two maps of possible destinations: one for signals sent before the astronaut crosses and one for signals sent after. The set of reachable destinations changes at the boundary, even though a nearby speed measurement does not.

blocks.heading: The boundary is about the future
blocks.body:
Outside the horizon, an outward-directed light signal can travel away and reach distant space. At the horizon, outward-directed light can at best stay on the boundary. Inside, even light aimed outward has no future path that crosses the horizon to the outside.

Anything carrying a message must follow a future path. Since even light cannot get out from inside, a rocket or radio signal cannot get out either.
blocks.example: You can cross the horizon inward, but you cannot send a message back across it outward once you are inside.

hints: Decide where each signal starts relative to the horizon.
Could adding power create an outward route that light itself cannot follow?
blocks.retry: Compare the two starting points rather than the power of the senders. A signal sent from outside can have distant space as a destination; one sent from inside cannot.

blocks.heading: Correct the claim
blocks.prompt: A friend says, “Gravity slows light to a stop at the event horizon.” In two sentences, correct the claim and explain why a flashlight switched on inside cannot send a signal out.
blocks.model: Light still moves at its usual speed when measured nearby; the horizon is not a place where it stops. Inside the horizon, even an outward-directed beam has no future path to distant space.

activities.title: A flashlight just inside
activities.prompt: Someone claims, “Gravity slows light to a stop at the event horizon.” An astronaut who has just crossed inside switches on a flashlight aimed outward. What happens?
activities.reveal: Light does not stop or slow down when measured nearby. The surprising part is that moving at light speed still does not give the beam a path to distant space.

options.text: The beam stops moving as soon as the astronaut switches it on.
options.feedback: The astronaut can measure the nearby beam moving at the usual speed of light.

options.text: The beam moves at the usual speed of light nearby, but never reaches distant space.
options.feedback: Yes. Its speed nearby and its eventual destination are different questions.

options.text: The beam reaches distant space because light is faster than anything else.
options.feedback: Being the fastest does not help if no future path from inside reaches distant space.

options.text: The beam crosses out of the horizon but then slows to a stop.
options.feedback: A light signal sent from inside cannot cross the horizon outward.

activities.title: Predict the routes
activities.prompt: Before tapping, predict which starting places let an outward light signal reach distant space: outside, exactly at the horizon, or inside? Then tap each place and trace the arrows to test your prediction.
activities.reveal: Only the signal starting outside has a route to distant space. At the horizon, outward light stays on the boundary; inside, its future path leads deeper, not outward across the boundary.

nodes.label: Outside
nodes.detail: From here, outward-directed light can travel away and eventually reach distant space.

nodes.label: At the horizon
nodes.detail: Light aimed outward from exactly here can at best remain on the boundary.

nodes.label: Inside
nodes.detail: Light can move outward nearby, but its future path cannot cross the horizon to the outside.

nodes.label: Distant space
nodes.detail: An observer far away can receive a signal that escapes.

nodes.label: Deeper inside
nodes.detail: Future paths from inside lead farther into the black hole.

questions.question: A falling astronaut measures the speed of a beam passing close by, first just outside the event horizon and then just inside. What happens to the astronaut’s local speed measurements?
options: The measurement is the usual speed of light on both sides.
The measurement drops to zero exactly at the horizon.
The measurement is higher inside because the beam is falling.
The measurement gradually decreases as the astronaut approaches the horizon.
questions.correctAnswer: The measurement is the usual speed of light on both sides.
questions.explanation: The astronaut measures light moving at its usual speed nearby on either side of the horizon. Crossing changes which distant places a signal can reach, not its locally measured speed.

questions.question: A probe outside the event horizon sends an outward radio pulse toward a distant spacecraft. A probe inside fires a powerful rocket outward and sends an outward radio pulse too. Which pulse can reach the spacecraft?
options: Both pulses, because radio waves travel at the speed of light.
Only the pulse sent from outside the horizon.
Only the pulse sent from inside, because its rocket adds speed.
Neither pulse, because the horizon blocks signals in both directions.
questions.correctAnswer: Only the pulse sent from outside the horizon.
questions.explanation: An outward signal from outside can reach distant space. From inside, no outward signal has a future path across the horizon, and the rocket cannot change that.

problems: The first check largely repeats the opening flashlight activity rather than testing a new application of the idea.
The diagram asks learners to trace paths, but its labels and details supply the conclusions, leaving little to work out.
The retry explanations restate the lesson’s distinction rather than offering a genuinely different way to understand it.

trace.blocks: activity > explain > check > activity > explain > check > reflect

problems: The route diagram says light at the horizon stays on the boundary, but provides no arrow showing that path, making the central visual test incomplete.
The two checks are useful but both mainly test the same outside-versus-inside distinction. Neither asks learners to reconcile an outward-pointed flashlight with a future path leading deeper inside.
